questions.question: Paying 6 units with coins {1, 3, 4} by taking the largest coin first gives 4 + 1 + 1. What does this show?
options: That the greedy algorithm has a bug in its remainder handling
That greedy change-making is not optimal for every denomination set, since 3 + 3 uses fewer coins
That the amount 6 cannot be made with these coins without a 2-unit coin
That greedy is optimal but the coin set should be sorted ascending instead
questions.explanation: The greedy ran correctly and produced a valid but suboptimal answer; the denomination set is not canonical. Sorting ascending would be a different and worse algorithm, and 6 is clearly makeable.

questions.question: In the exchange argument for earliest-finish-first interval scheduling, why can the first interval of any optimal solution be swapped for the greedy's first pick?
options: Because the greedy pick is the shortest interval, so it fits wherever the optimal's first interval fit
Because the greedy pick ends no later, so everything after the optimal's first interval still starts after the greedy pick ends
Because the greedy pick starts earliest, so no interval in the optimal solution can precede it
Because every optimal solution has the same size, so any interval can replace any other
questions.explanation: The swap preserves disjointness precisely because the greedy interval has the earliest end: the rest of the optimal set started at or after the replaced interval's end, hence after the greedy's end. Shortest-first and earliest-start-first are the wrong criteria and both have counterexamples.

questions.question: Why is it safe for Huffman's algorithm to merge the two least frequent symbols first?
options: Because in some optimal tree those two symbols are sibling leaves at the deepest level, so merging them loses nothing
Because the two rarest symbols contribute the fewest bits, so their codes do not affect the total
Because merging in frequency order guarantees the tree is balanced and therefore minimal
Because the heap always returns the two most recently inserted nodes first
questions.explanation: The exchange argument shows that swapping any deeper symbol with a rarer one never increases total length, so the two rarest can be assumed to be deepest siblings; collapsing them into one node yields a smaller instance of the same problem. Huffman trees are usually unbalanced, and the rare symbols' codes do matter, just less.

questions.question: The minResources algorithm checks only whether the lane with the earliest end time is free before opening a new lane. Why is that sufficient?
options: Because lanes are closed in the order they were opened, so the earliest-ending lane is the oldest
Because the heap stores at most one lane and the check is therefore exhaustive
Because intervals are processed in order of end time, so earlier lanes always finish first
Because if the earliest-ending lane is still busy at the new start, every other lane ends later and is busy too
questions.explanation: The heap's minimum is the earliest end time among all lanes; if even that lane has not freed up, none has. Intervals are processed by start time, not end time, and the heap holds one entry per open lane.

questions.question: A payments team configures a new market whose coinage is {1, 3, 6, 12, 24, 30, 60, 240} and keeps the largest-first dispensing algorithm. What should they have run first?
options: A benchmark of the greedy against a brute-force search for amounts up to the largest denomination
A verification that the denominations are sorted and that a 1-unit coin exists
A check that each denomination divides the next, which guarantees greedy optimality
The Kozen-Zaks canonicality check: compare greedy to the DP optimum for every amount below 240 + 60
questions.explanation: Greedy is optimal for all amounts if and only if it is optimal for every amount below the sum of the two largest denominations; this set fails at 48 (30+12+6 versus 24+24). Divisibility is sufficient but not necessary (US coins do not satisfy it), and a 1-coin only guarantees every amount is makeable, not optimally.

questions.question: A design document proposes filling payout batches by 'largest fee tier first' to minimise processor fees under a tiered schedule. What is the right review response?
options: Approve: a greedy allocation is optimal whenever the cost function is monotone non-decreasing in the batch size
Approve: tier schedules are canonical by construction because each tier's range is nested inside the next one
Ask for an exchange argument or a test against a DP oracle, because tier boundaries behave like non-canonical coin denominations
Reject: greedy algorithms are never an appropriate tool for cost-minimisation problems and dynamic programming must be used
questions.explanation: Step-function costs create exactly the structure where largest-first overpays, as {1, 3, 4} does for coins; the burden is on the proposal to show the greedy-choice property or to test it against the true optimum. Monotonicity is not enough, and greedy is optimal for many cost problems (Huffman, MST) when the proof exists.
